html:
In 1796 the English country doctor Edward Jenner showed that infecting someone with cowpox, a mild disease of cows, protected them against smallpox. It was the start of vaccination.

Smallpox killed a large share of children in Europe and left survivors scarred or blind. The best defence before Jenner was variolation, giving people a mild case of smallpox itself, a practice brought to England from the Ottoman world. It worked but was risky.

Milkmaids were said not to catch smallpox after having cowpox. In May 1796 Jenner took matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, and put it into a cut on the arm of a boy, James Phipps. Weeks later he exposed the boy to smallpox, and he did not fall ill. Jenner published his findings in 1798.

The method spread across the world within a few years. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin for cow, and Louis Pasteur later widened it to all such treatments. Vaccination finally wiped smallpox out: the last natural case was in 1977.
sum: In 1796 the English country doctor Edward Jenner showed that infecting someone with cowpox, a mild disease of cows, protected them against smallpox. It was the start of vaccination.
